keep: The idea is named in one line up front: water speeds up through a narrowing and its pressure drops there, and measuring the drop makes a flow meter.
It starts from continuity, as the misconception research asks, before any Bernoulli: flow = area × speed, worked with real numbers, 20 cm² at 2 m/s is 4 L/s, so a 5 cm² throat runs at 8 m/s.
The rule is stated in words and worked: pressure is energy per cubic metre, speed carries ½ρv² per cubic metre, the sum stays the same, so the throat drops ½ × 1025 × (8² − 2²), about 30.8 kPa.

The picture is the brief's venturi: a throat and a flow slider, dots stretching out in the throat, A × v labels equal, three columns that drop and recover, a flow readout worked back from the drop, a measure switch and a smooth or eddying switch.

Each misconception has a puzzle with its own wrong pick: pressure rising with flow (screens 3 and 7), Bernoulli used without continuity (screen 7 starts from areas, with the pipe's speed left out as a pick), the ratio upside down (screen 5), the drop in step with flow (screen 9).
Every number is a control, an assumed example, a constant or computed from A × v or ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²); the mixed puzzles reach back to absolute pressure (lesson 3) and ρgh (lesson 5).

The analogy, one current through a thinner length of cable, reproduces same flow and higher density at the narrowing, and its breaks names the real difference: a cable's drop is lost as heat, a venturi's mostly comes back.
fix: False absolute: 'The only push on the water is the pressure of the water around it.' Gravity acts in a pipe that climbs, and the walls drag on it. Say along a level pipe the forward push comes from the pressure of the water around it.

False absolute and the contested point flattened: 'Below about 2000 the flow is smooth, and above about 4000 it eddies.' Sources put the switch in different places. Teach it as not agreed: most put smooth flow below about 2000 and eddies above about 4000, with no single switch point between.
A condition missing from the rule: p + ½ρv² stays constant along a level pipe. Say so, and that a climbing pipe adds a height share, the ρgh from Pressure in liquids, as a textbook addition.

Interactive shows the effect, not the cause: the columns show the drop but nothing shows why. Add a highlighted slug of water entering the throat with two pressure arrows, the one behind longer than the one in front, swapping as it leaves. Screen 8 also lacks the quantity form: add a small plot of drop against flow, a curve rising as the flow squared, with a dot at the current flow.

Screen 3's prediction lacks the misconception as a pick. Make the choices: the throat's column stands lowest, the throat's column stands tallest because the water is squeezed, or all three stand level.
The teaching-model sentence sits after the Reynolds talk, where it reads as if about eddies. Move it to the end of the Bernoulli paragraph, beside the pressure coming back.
Two colon chains ('Pressure is itself energy per cubic metre: pushing…', 'That is continuity: area × speed…'). Split into whole sentences.
Practice names only the venturi. Dan will meet orifice plates: add one line, as a textbook addition, that a plate with a hole works the same way more cheaply but loses more of the drop for good.
